headline: The July jobs report lands before this morning's open with S&P 500 futures up about 0.1%, after Iran said it struck targets in the Strait of Hormuz and Brent crude extended above $83 overnight.
stance: Today is the week's verdict: the July jobs report — consensus near 83,000 jobs with unemployment at 4.2% — arrives before the open, after a week in which private-sector hiring badly missed. Overnight the other pillar moved the wrong way: Iran said it struck targets in the Strait of Hormuz and a draft before its parliament would tighten shipping conditions, pushing Brent above $83 for a second day of gains. Midweek futures pricing put roughly 62% odds on a quarter-point hike at the September 16 meeting — a soft print pulls that down; a hot one, with oil re-accelerating, cements it.

news.head: Strait strikes stall the reopening story
news.body: Iran said it struck what it described as hostile targets in the Strait of Hormuz after explosions were reported near Qeshm Island, a day after signaling a shipping-route deal with Oman was close — and a draft before Iran's parliament would impose stricter conditions on commercial shipping than markets had expected.

news.head: Oil extends the climb
news.body: Brent rose above $83 early Friday — about $83.60 by ~6am ET, up roughly 1% — building on Thursday's 3.8% jump to an $82.49 settle; US crude sat near $78.20 overnight.

news.head: Jobs day: consensus 83,000
news.body: The official July employment report is due before the open; forecasts center on about 83,000 jobs added with unemployment holding at 4.2%, after this week's 44,000 private-payrolls miss and against June's 57,000.

news.head: Yen gives back intervention gains
news.body: The yen weakened to about ¥158.5 per dollar overnight (~6am ET), reported early Friday as having surrendered nearly half its gains from the joint US-Japan currency intervention; the pair now sits in the 85th percentile of its three-year range, a stretch reading that turned fresh this week.

news.head: Gold eases despite the strait
news.body: Gold traded near $4,292 an ounce early Friday (~6am ET), down from about $4,342 Thursday evening, even as crude climbed; silver sat near $61.60.

news.head: Insiders cluster in small-cap pharma
news.body: Filings dated Wednesday show six distinct insiders at one small-cap drug developer (MBRX) buying about $3.4 million of stock and nine buyers at another (CAMP) about $3.3 million — two of the week's largest insider-buying clusters.

implications: The print sets the September path: midweek pricing implied roughly 62% odds of a quarter-point hike at the September 16 meeting — a soft number after the 44,000 private-payrolls miss pulls that down, while a hot one lands on top of a fresh oil impulse.

The overnight strikes and the stricter-shipping draft cut against the reopening hopes that had capped crude, and the bond market's bet that the energy shock fades is eroding at the margin: the 10-year breakeven inflation rate closed Thursday at 2.26%, up from 2.22% Wednesday.
The options market carries little cushion into the number: the VIX closed Thursday at 15.2, down from 15.8 Wednesday — equity volatility declined into the event rather than bracing for it.

Positioning: New in the latest weekly futures data: speculators added grain longs — corn at the 87th percentile of the past three years, soybeans at the 88th — while natural-gas specs went extended short (8th percentile) with commercial hedgers on the other side; wheat longs sit a third week at the 99th. The Treasury-belly longs flagged yesterday (5-year at the 97th percentile, 2-year at the 87th) remain the standing exposure into this morning's print.

watch.head: July jobs report (before the open)
watch.body: Consensus near 83,000 with unemployment at 4.2%, against June's 57,000 and this week's 44,000 private-payrolls miss — the decisive input for the September 16 meeting.

watch.head: Hormuz next moves
watch.body: Whether Iran's parliament advances the stricter shipping draft and whether the still-unannounced Oman corridor deal lands — the two headlines that could swing crude in either direction after overnight strikes.

watch.head: Software follow-through at the open
watch.body: Thursday evening's after-market surges — Atlassian roughly +33%, Doximity about +66%, Twilio and Cloudflare about +16% each — face their first regular-session test today; whether they hold is the cleanest read on enterprise-software demand.

watch.head: Yen at ¥158.5
watch.body: With nearly half the intervention gains reported gone, a hot US jobs number would press the pair further while a soft one gives Tokyo breathing room.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: The biggest change overnight: the Hormuz de-escalation story stalled. Iran said it struck what it called hostile targets in the strait after explosions were reported near Qeshm Island, and a draft before its parliament would set stricter conditions on commercial shipping than markets had anticipated — Brent pushed above $83 early Friday (about $83.60 by ~6am ET) after settling at $82.49 Thursday, up 3.8%.

The July employment report is due before the open: consensus centers on about 83,000 jobs with unemployment at 4.2%, after June's 57,000 and a 44,000 private-payrolls reading for July that badly missed expectations earlier this week.

Yields rose into it: the 10-year Treasury closed Thursday at 4.69% (4.63% Wednesday), the 2-year at 4.25%, leaving the curve at +44 basis points; midweek futures pricing implied roughly 62% odds of a quarter-point hike at the September 16 meeting.
Inflation expectations are creeping up with oil: the 10-year breakeven rate closed Thursday at 2.26% versus 2.22% Wednesday, while the 10-year real (inflation-adjusted) yield closed at 2.43%.

In currencies, the yen weakened overnight to about ¥158.5 per dollar (~6am ET), reported early Friday as having given back nearly half its gains from the joint US-Japan intervention; the dollar index closed Thursday just under 100 and the euro sat near $1.15 overnight.
Gold eased to about $4,292 early Friday (~6am ET) from roughly $4,342 Thursday evening even as crude climbed; silver traded near $61.60.
sections.positioning: Standing backdrop into the print, not new: speculators remain extended long the belly of the Treasury curve — 5-year futures at the 97th percentile of the past three years, 2-year at the 87th in the latest weekly data. In plain English: the bond market's most piled-into bet is that rates fall, and a hot payrolls number is what would punish it.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: S&P 500 futures were up about 0.1% early Friday (~5am ET) ahead of the print, after Thursday's oil-driven slip: the S&P 500 closed down 0.2% at 7,709.96, the Dow down 0.9% at 53,885.10, and the Nasdaq down 0.1% at 26,348.35.
The options market goes into jobs day priced calm: the VIX closed Thursday at 15.2, down from 15.8 at Wednesday's close.
Breadth at Thursday's close: about 65% of S&P 500 members traded above their 50-day trend line, and 55% of Nasdaq-100 members did.

Fresh insider buying clustered in small-cap pharma — filings dated Wednesday show six distinct insiders at MBRX buying about $3.4 million of stock and nine at CAMP about $3.3 million — and Thursday's newest filings added a roughly $588,000 purchase at ATTO.

single_name.note: (Taiwan Semiconductor — the main contract manufacturer of advanced chips) - company insiders filed a fresh purchase this week, the shares trade above their 200-day trend line, and the setup's dark-pool and options signals are live after 40 sessions on the scan list.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: Credit is taking the oil re-escalation in stride so far: the high-yield-over-investment-grade spread sat at 275 basis points at Wednesday's close, versus 287 in late July, with investment-grade spreads at 78 basis points.

Short-term funding remains quiet: the key bank-funding spreads closed Wednesday near 1 basis point, and the commercial-paper funding spread's latest reading eased to 22 basis points from 25 at end-July.

The system's spare-cash cushion is still gone: the overnight reverse-repo facility held $1.4 billion Thursday, with bank reserves at $2,993.3 billion and the Treasury's cash account at $907.3 billion in Wednesday's weekly snapshot.
Bank lending keeps expanding in the background — commercial-bank credit rose 6.11% year-over-year in the latest weekly reading (late July), and the average rate on new syndicated loans sat at 7.08%.
